'''Amyand David Buckingham''' {{postnominals|country=AUS|size=100%|CBE|FRS|FAA}} (28 January 1930 in [[Pymble, New South Wales]] – 4 February 2021)  was an Australian chemist, with primary expertise in [[chemical physics]].<ref>{{Cite journal | author = Anon| doi = 10.1080/00268979600100491 | title = Amyand David Buckingham | journal = Molecular Physics | volume = 87 | issue = 4 | pages = 711–724 | year = 1996 |bibcode = 1996MolPh..87..711. | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ch.cam.ac.uk/news/david-buckingham-1930-2021|title=A. David Buckingham 1930 - 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=David Buckingham - Biography |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/david-buckingham-11157/ |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=10 February 2021 |quote=Professor David Buckingham CBE FRS died on 4 February 2021.}}</ref>

==Life and career==
David Buckingham attended [[Barker College]] in Sydney.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Clary |first1=David C. |last2=Orr |first2=Brian J. |title=Amyand David Buckingham. 28 January 1930—4 February 2021 |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsbm/article/doi/10.1098/rsbm.2021.0026/116182/Amyand-David-Buckingham-28-January-1930-4-February |website=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |publisher=The Royal Society Publishing |access-date=25 March 2026}}</ref> He then obtained a [[Bachelor of Science]] and [[Master of Science]], under Professor [[Raymond Le Fevre]],<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Aroney | first1 = M. J. | last2 = Buckingham | first2 = A. D. | authorlink2 = A. David Buckingham| doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1988.0014 | title = Raymond James Wood Le Fèvre. 1 April 1905-26 August 1986 | journal = Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society | volume = 34 | pages = 374 | year = 1988 | doi-access = free }}</ref> from the [[University of Sydney]] and a [[PhD]] from the [[University of Cambridge]] supervised by [[John Pople]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Buckingham | first1 = A. D. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2006.0021  | doi-access = free| title = Sir John Anthony Pople. 31 October 1925 -- 15 March 2004: Elected FRS 1961 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 52 | pages =  299–310| year = 2006 | s2cid = 68810170 }}</ref> He was an 1851 Exhibition Senior Student in the [[Physical and Theoretical Chemistry Laboratory|Physical Chemistry Laboratory]] at the [[University of Oxford]] from 1955 to 1957, Lecturer and then Student (Fellow) at [[Christ Church, Oxford]] from 1955 to 1965 and University Lecturer in the Inorganic Chemistry Laboratory from 1958 to 1965. He was Professor of Theoretical Chemistry at the [[University of Bristol]] from 1965 to 1969. He was appointed Professor of Chemistry at the University of Cambridge in 1969.

He was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1975,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Clary|first1=David C.|last2=Orr|first2=Brian J.|title=Amyand David Buckingham. 28 January 1930—4 February 2021|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|year=2022 |volume=72|pages=77–99 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2021.0026 |s2cid=244923085 |doi-access=free}}</ref> a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] in 1986 and a Foreign Associate of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] in 1992. He was a member of the [[International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iaqms.org/members/buckingham.php |title=A. David Buckingham: International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science |archivedate=20 February 2012 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120220050027/http://www.iaqms.org/members/buckingham.php |url-status=live |df=dmy }}</ref> Buckingham was elected to the Australian Academy of Science in 2008 as a Corresponding Fellow.

He was awarded the first [[Ahmed Zewail]] Prize in Molecular Sciences<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2006-10/e-eat100406.php |title=Elsevier announces the winner of the first Ahmed Zewail Prize in Molecular Sciences |archivedate=25 August 2012 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120825090640/http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2006-10/e-eat100406.php |url-status=live |df=dmy }}</ref> for pioneering contributions to the molecular sciences in 2006.

He won the [[Harrie Massey Medal and Prize]] in 1995.

He also played 10 [[first-class cricket|first class cricket]] matches for [[Cambridge University Cricket Club|Cambridge University]] and [[Free Foresters Cricket Club|Free Foresters]] between 1955 and 1960, scoring 349 runs including two half-centuries at an average of 18.36.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.espncricinfo.com/england/content/player/10115.html |title=A. David Buckingham &#124; England Cricket &#124; Cricket Players and Officials &#124; ESPN Cricinfo |archivedate=13 May 2018 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20180513225125/http://www.espncricinfo.com/england/content/player/10115.html |url-status=live |df=dmy }}</ref>  He was President of [[Cambridge University Cricket Club]] between 1990 and 2009.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://cucc.net/index.php/cucc-presidents-2/|title=CUCC Presidents}}</ref>

Professor Buckingham finished his career as Emeritus Professor of Chemistry at the [[University of Cambridge]], [[United Kingdom]] and Emeritus Fellow at [[Pembroke College, Cambridge]].

==Scientific contributions==
Professor Buckingham's research has focussed on the measurement and understanding of the electric, magnetic and optical properties of molecules; as well as on the theory of [[intermolecular forces]].

Initially he worked on [[dielectric]] properties of liquids, such as [[Dipole#Molecular dipoles|dipole moments]] of molecules in both solution and gas phases. He developed the theory of the interaction of molecules in liquids and gases with external electric and magnetic fields. In 1959, he proposed a direct method of measurement of molecular [[Quadrupole#Electric quadrupole|quadrupole]] moments of molecules (measured in [[Buckingham (unit)|buckinghams]]),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Buckingham |first1=A.D. |title=Direct Method of Measuring Molecular Quadrupole Moments |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |date=1959 |volume=30 |issue=6 |pages=1580–1585 |doi=10.1063/1.1730242 |bibcode=1959JChPh..30.1580B }}</ref> which he demonstrated experimentally in 1963 on the [[carbon dioxide]] molecule.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Buckingham | first1 = A. D. | authorlink = A. David Buckingham| last2 = Disch | first2 = R. L. | doi = 10.1098/rspa.1963.0088 | title = The Quadrupole Moment of the Carbon Dioxide Molecule | journal = Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences | volume = 273 | issue = 1353 | pages = 275 | year = 1963 |bibcode = 1963RSPSA.273..275B | s2cid = 97286311 }}</ref> In 1960, he developed theories of [[solvent effects]] on [[NMR spectroscopy|nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra]] and [[Molecular vibration|vibrational spectra]] of molecules.<ref>Buckingham A.D., Schaffer T. and Schneider W.G. ''Solvent effects in nuclear magnetic resonance spectra'', J. Chem. Phys., 32, 1960, 1227-1233, https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1730879</ref><ref>Buckingham A.D., ''Solvent effects in vibrational spectroscopy'', Trans. Faraday Society, 56, 1960, 753-760, https://doi.org/10.1039/TF9605600753</ref> In 1962 he considered the effect on NMR spectra of molecular orientation in a strong electric field, and developed a method to determine the absolute sign of the [[J-coupling|spin-spin coupling]] constant.<ref>Buckingham A.D. and Lovering E.G., ''Effects of a strong electric field on NMR spectra. The absolute sign of the spin coupling constant'', Transactions Faraday Society, 58, 2077-2081 (1962), https://doi.org/10.1039/TF9625802077</ref> In 1968, he determined the first accurate values of [[hyperpolarizability]] using the [[Kerr effect]].<ref>Buckingham A.D. and Hibbard P., ''Polarizability and Hyperpolarizability of the Helium Atom'', Symp. Faraday Society, 2, 1968, 41-47, https://doi.org/10.1039/SF9680200041</ref> In 1971 Buckingham and [[Laurence Barron]] pioneered the study of [[Raman optical activity]], due to differences in the [[Raman scattering]] of [[Circular polarization|left and right-polarized light]] by [[chirality (chemistry)|chiral]] molecules.<ref>Barron L.D. and Buckingham A.D., ''Rayleigh and Raman Scattering from optically active molecules'', Molecular Physics, 20, 1111-1119 (1971), https://doi.org/10.1080/00268977100101091</ref>

In the 1980s, he showed the importance of long-range intermolecular forces in determining the structure and properties of small molecule [[Cluster chemistry|clusters]], with particular applications in biological [[macromolecule]]s. In 1990 he predicted the linear effect of an electric field on the [[reflection of light]] at [[Interface (chemistry)|interfaces]].<ref>Buckingham A.D. ''Linear and nonlinear light scattering from the surface of liquids'', Australian Journal of Physics, 43, 617-624 (1990), https://www.publish.csiro.au/ph/pdf/PH900617</ref> In 1995, he proved that the sum of the rotational strengths of all [[vibrational transition]]s from the ground state of a chiral molecule is zero.<ref>Buckingham A.D. ''The theoretical background to vibrational optical activity'', Faraday Discussions, 99, 1-12 (1994)[https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1994/fd/fd9949900001 Abstract]</ref>

==Personal life==
In July 1964, David Buckingham sailed from Southampton to Montréal, to take up a research post in Ottawa. On the voyage he met Jillian Bowles, a physiotherapist who was heading to a post in British
Columbia. They were engaged in January 1965 and married at [[Christ Church Cathedral, Oxford]] six months later. They were married for over 55 years, and had three children: Lucy Elliot and Mark Vincent, born in Bristol, and Alice Susan born in Cambridge. Between them they had eight grandchildren: Carola, Peter, Oliver, William, Patrick, Anna, Samuel and Maeve.

David Buckingham died in Cambridge on 4 February 2021, seven days after his 91st birthday; he was survived by Jill, their children and grandchildren.
